title: Acid Graphics vs Neo-Brutalism
lede: Both are loud, both use hard edges and flat colour, and both are frequently described as anti-design. One is dark and acidic; the other is light and sweet.
verdict: Acid graphics runs on black, one lime accent and tightly packed negative tracking, with a fixed 5-degree skew. Neo-brutalism runs on cream, five pastel fills and 8px hard shadows, with everything upright.
brief: The shapes are similar enough that a screenshot can be mistaken for the other: thick borders, no gradients, flat colour, type doing most of the work. The temperature is completely different.

Acid graphics compresses: letter-spacing at minus 0.03 to 0.04em, a headline skewed about five degrees, offsets held at a fixed 6px so the misalignment reads as a system rather than an accident. Neo-brutalism expands: cream ground, five candy fills, 8px shadows, and every block sitting squarely on the grid with no rotation at all.

dimensions.name: Reading comfort
dimensions.b: Moderate — pastels are gentler than lime

whenA: The audience is young, the content is music or events, and the page is a poster rather than a document
You want a single loud screen — a launch hero, a cover, a teaser
The brand can afford to be disliked by part of the audience
whenB: The page has to stay usable for several minutes rather than five seconds
You need multiple cards or items differentiated by colour
The brand is playful but still wants to be trusted with a transaction
promptDelta: Name the ground first: black for acid, cream for neo-brutalism. That one line does more than the style name, because both names are vague. Then give the offset as a number and say whether it is a shadow or a displacement — acid displaces the element, neo-brutalism hangs a hard shadow beneath it. Finally, state the palette count: one accent for acid, five named pastels for neo-brutalism. A model asked for either without a count will produce four or five colours and land somewhere in between.
